title: Going for two: the kick, the 2-point try, and college overtime (and how Rutgers won with no time left)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files. So there are no new misses to target. This lesson takes a new concept from Saturday's two biggest finishes.

The big idea: after a touchdown, the offense gets one extra play, called the try.It can kick for 1 point. Or it can run one play from close to the goal line for 2 points.The kick almost always works. The 2-point play works about half the time.

The end zone is at the top. Yellow = the college line (the 3) and Rutgers' winning pass. White = the NFL lines.

  1. A · College: the 3-yard line. Both the kick and the 2-point try start here. The kick is short, about 20 yards.
  2. B · NFL 2-point try: the 2-yard line. One play. Run or pass. Score and it's 2 points. Fail and it's 0.NFL teams convert about half of them.
  3. C · NFL kick: the 15-yard line. The NFL moved the kick back in 2015. It's now a 33-yard kick, made about 94% of the time.
  4. D · Saturday's real example. Rutgers trailed Penn State 24-17. AJ Surace hit Ben Black III for a 3-yard TD as time ran out: 24-23.A kick ties it and goes to overtime. Greg Schiano went for 2 instead. Surace hit DK Gilley. Rutgers won 25-24.

Why go for 2 to win? Compare the two paths. Kick: about 95% to tie, then overtime against a team favored by 24.5 points.Go for 2: one snap, about a coin flip, and the game is over.An underdog with a banged-up QB may have less than a 50% chance in overtime. So one coin flip can be the better bet.

College overtime rules: each team gets one possession from the opponent's 25-yard line.From the 2nd overtime, a team that scores a TD must go for 2. No kicks.From the 3rd overtime, there are no more drives. Each team runs one 2-point play, back and forth, until one scores and the other doesn't.Saturday: Michigan and UCLA were 10-10 after regulation. Michigan won 18-16 on a 2-point try in the 3rd overtime.

Why it matters for bets: a 2-point try moves the score by 2, not 1. Saturday it moved Rutgers' total from 23 to 25 and flipped the moneyline.Overtime counts for totals and spreads on Kalshi and at most books. Michigan-UCLA still went under (34), but Washington-Indiana went over only because of OT.Late in a game, a team down 8 needs a TD and a 2-pointer just to tie. That's why "down 8" feels closer than it is.

For your Film Room drill: a 2-point try is a normal snap. Log it run or pass like any other.Clues: a short field squeezes the defense, so offenses love quick passes to the corner or a QB sprint-out.Rutgers threw. Michigan's winning try was its last play of the night. Watch for it on Thanksgiving: three NFL games, plenty of late tries.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 60 showed fourth-and-long late in a game: the sticks decide the call. A 2-point try is the same idea at the goal line. One snap, a known distance, and the coach weighs a sure thing against a bigger payoff.

Video: search YouTube for "Rutgers Penn State 2 point conversion Surace Gilley" and "college football overtime rules explained."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

quiz.q: In college, where is the ball snapped for a 2-point try?
quiz.w: College tries, kick or 2-point, start at the 3. The NFL uses the 2 for 2-point tries.

quiz.q: Where is an NFL extra-point kick snapped?
quiz.w: Since 2015 the NFL snaps the kick at the 15, so it's a 33-yard kick.

quiz.q: Rutgers scored to make it 24-23 with no time left. Why go for 2?
o: One coin-flip play can beat a long-shot overtime
quiz.w: The kick only ties. A big underdog may have less than a 50% chance in OT, so one roughly 50% play can be better.

quiz.q: In college, what happens from the 3rd overtime on?
o: Each team runs one 2-point play, alternating
The game ends in a tie
quiz.w: From the 3rd OT, teams trade single 2-point plays. Michigan beat UCLA that way, 18-16.
